selected_mechanism.name: Stak Energy North Slope AI Campus — DNR Best-Interest to Army Corps CWA Section 404 Permitting Stack

news_trigger.headline: Alaska's North Slope proposed as home for massive AI data center
news_trigger.verbatim_span: State preliminary approval granted for land lease off Dalton Highway. Project currently exists only in planning phase. Requires navigation of land use and permitting processes. Construction of the Stak Energy Campus is scheduled to begin in summer 2026... Initial operations are expected to begin by late 2028.

selected_mechanism.one_line_definition: A sequential state-and-federal permitting stack that any developer must navigate to build a large-scale AI data center on Alaska state land in the North Slope — running from the Alaska DNR best-interest finding through public appeal standing to a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Clean Water Act Section 404 authorization that must be obtained before any ground is broken.

layers.layer_name: Alaska DNR Best-Interest Finding and 50-Year Land Lease
layers.what_it_does: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas issues a preliminary best-interest finding under AS 38.05.070(d) determining the proposed 715.4-acre lease to Stak Energy Corporation is in the state's best interest. The preliminary finding triggers the mandatory public comment period and, if sustained, leads to a final finding and 50-year lease execution. Without a final DNR finding, no lease is issued and no construction can begin.
layers.controlling_actor: Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Oil and Gas — Permitting Section (Commissioner-delegated authority); institutional role persists regardless of the Commissioner's identity

layers.layer_name: Public Comment and Administrative Appeal Window
layers.what_it_does: Any party that submits written comments to DNR by 4:30 PM Alaska Daylight Time on June 15, 2026 earns standing to appeal the Final Best-Interest Finding under AS 38.05.035(i)-(m) to the Alaska Superior Court. A successful appeal can halt the lease indefinitely. The June 15 deadline is the structural gate: miss it and appellate standing is forfeited.
layers.controlling_actor: Public commenters (standing gate) and Alaska Superior Court (appellate authority) — institutional mechanism, not a named individual

layers.layer_name: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers CWA Section 404 Authorization
layers.what_it_does: Stak Energy must obtain a federal Clean Water Act Section 404 authorization from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers before discharging approximately 7 million cubic yards of gravel fill — nearly twice the volume authorized for the Willow oil project — to elevate power plants and computing systems off the tundra. No application has been filed as of May 2026. The Corps administers this permit program nationally; the Alaska District holds jurisdiction for this project. This is the binary gate before any physical construction.
layers.controlling_actor: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Alaska District (POA) — the District Engineer holds statutory permit authority under 33 U.S.C. § 1344; institutional role, not a named incumbent

chokepoint.layer_name: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers CWA Section 404 Authorization
chokepoint.controlling_actor: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Alaska District, District Engineer (institutional role under 33 U.S.C. § 1344)
chokepoint.binary_decision: Authorize or deny the Section 404 permit for approximately 7 million cubic yards of gravel fill — no permit means no gravel pad, no gravel pad means no construction, no construction means no data center. No application has been filed as of May 2026; the Corps has sole statutory authority to issue or deny this authorization within its jurisdiction, and no other federal or state actor can substitute.

selected_mechanism.structural_read: The Stak Energy North Slope AI campus exists today as a DNR preliminary finding on paper and a summer 2026 construction timeline in press releases. The actual permitting machine has three sequential gates before a shovel touches the ground: DNR must finalize the best-interest finding (June 15 comment deadline approaching), the public appeal window must close without a successful court challenge, and — most critically — the Army Corps must authorize a gravel fill that is unprecedented in scale for a non-resource-extraction project in Arctic Alaska. No Section 404 application has been filed. The Corps typically takes 12-24 months to process a standard 404 permit; a project of this complexity and gravel volume, with no precedent and no application filed, cannot realistically receive authorization in time for a summer 2026 construction start. The chokepoint is not Stak's business plan or its CEO — it is the federal permitting machine, which moves on its own timeline and requires environmental review under NEPA before the Corps can act.
selected_mechanism.forward_implication: Any Alaska AI infrastructure investor or operator evaluating the North Slope corridor should treat the Army Corps Section 404 application filing date — not the DNR lease date or Stak's press timeline — as the real project clock. Until an application is filed and a NEPA determination is initiated, a summer 2026 construction start is structurally impossible. Watch the Corps' Alaska District public notice register (not filed as of May 30, 2026) as the definitive early-warning signal for whether this project is real or a placeholder narrative.
selected_mechanism.ak_consequence: Alaska AI data center sector: Stak Energy's proposed 3 GW North Slope AI campus — which would be the largest AI compute facility in Alaska — cannot break ground under its stated summer 2026 timeline without a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Section 404 authorization that has not yet been applied for, creating a multi-year permitting gap that any capital allocator or infrastructure developer must underwrite before committing to the North Slope AI corridor.
